title: Priya and the Sad Moonpetals
markdown:
The moonpetal blossoms in the garden used to shimmer, silvery white under moonlight, their perfume a lullaby. Lately the pale petals curled inward. The fragrance was a fainter whisper. A soft concern settled over Priya.

She watered them well. They still looked sad. Flint, her little terrier, nudged her hand, thinking the soil needed loosening. He wiggled his nose near the roots until she worried he would disturb them.

Dr Ada Brook knelt beside her, smile warm as cocoa. “Sometimes digging isn’t the answer. Let’s watch what they are telling us.” She pointed to thread-like tendrils in the soil. “Roots. Quiet straws, drawing water and goodness. Also anchors, so the plant can stand.”

Priya leaned closer, imagining the reach downward.

“This part” — Ada traced the pale green stem — “is a gentle elevator. Water and food from the roots up to leaves and flowers.” Priya watched as if in a dream. A tiny droplet seemed to climb like a miniature stream.

“The leaves are busy kitchens. Sunlight, air, water — the food that keeps the plant alive and helps it bloom.” Priya pictured little chefs making sunshine snacks, then stopped herself smiling; the leaves still hung shy.

She gasped. Some roots looked squashed, unable to stretch. The leaves were not reaching for the sun. Flint, eager, had nudged small pebbles against the roots. The pot sat in a shady corner, where moonpetals could not make enough food.

With her smallest trowel Priya loosened the soil, moving pebbles softly. Ada nodded. They shifted the pot to a warm windowsill where daylight would find it. Flint watched, tail still, as if he understood that watching could be help.

Slowly, as if waking from a nap, the blossoms lifted their heads. Silvery white returned. They straightened toward the light. Relief warmed Priya. Roots drank, stems carried, leaves made food, flowers bloomed. Each part had a job; the jobs needed room and sun.

Evening laid peaceful shadows. Priya sat near the pot. Flint curled at her feet. The flowers did not murmur thanks. The crickets started anyway. She left the trowel clean on the sill, where she could see it if the petals curled again.
